content.title: Official Blind Review #3
content.review_assessment:_thoroughness_in_paper: I read the paper at least twice and used my best judgement in assessing the paper.
content.review:
This paper involves several common-seen techniques of domain adaptation, source label guided classifier training with a softmax cross entropy loss, GRL guided domain discrepancy minimization with a domain discriminator, and label propagation with manifold learning.

The label propagation is the novelty of this work, which proposes a cycle consistency on the source labels, for local class manifold alignment.

The local manifold consistency loss in Eq.(4) seems to have the similar physical insight with Eq. (3), but introducing the GAN model, which is similar to the perceptural loss. 

I have some concerns.
The LGAN from the paper is a pre-trained generator without re-training, as can be seen from Eq.(5) and (5). So, how do you have a control on its adaptation of LGAN to the DA problem of this paper? I also think that this seems to be an incremental method by simply introducing LGAN into the traditional DA model for data augmentation.

From Eq.(6), the L_cycle and L_local are the new terms based on the traditional DA. Actually, I have some concern that because of the domain distribution difference, the similarity matrix Wts between target and source data cannot well reflect the true similarity. I understand that the L_dann loss can align the marginal distribution across domains. So, this is an problem of "chicken first or egg first", which depends on the training strategy of the model.

The experimental comparison is not strong between the proposed and the CDAN. Actually, there lacks of an ablation analysis, by removing the L_local and L_cycle.

At least, from the given experiments, the performance of the proposed losses is not significant, with at most 0.5 percent improvement.

content.title: Response to Reviewer #3 (Part 1/2)
content.comment:
We thank the reviewer for the constructive comments.

Q1) The LGAN from the paper is a pre-trained generator without re-training, as can be seen from Eq.(5) and (5). So, how do you have a control on its adaptation of LGAN to the DA problem of this paper? I also think that this seems to be an incremental method by simply introducing LGAN into the traditional DA model for data augmentation.  

A1) We agree that L_local can be perceived as data augmentation, but we also would like to emphasize that it is a manifold regularization (Simard et al., 1992; Kumar et al.,
2017; Qi et al., 2018). LGAN is employed here because it is specialized to capture local manifold structure. Any generator that approximates the local manifold structure can also be applied. The main contribution on L_local is pursuing manifold consistency to unsupervised domain adaptation problem. The generator works on the data manifold, so it does not need to adapt once pretraining is done. 
A similar idea can be found in DIRT-T (Shu et al., 2018) which adapted VAT loss [1] to constrain classifier to be locally-Lipschitz. The difference between DIRT-T and our model is that ours imposes consistency within the data manifold whereas DIRT-T finds it on the whole input dimension. This difference results in the superior performance of our method as reported in Table 1. We also provide an ablation study that applied VAT loss instead of L_local to claim the effectiveness of L_local as below. The experiments were run 5 times. 

		<Comparison between VAT loss and L_local>
Source			MNIST	         	MNIST	   		USPS       		SVHN	  		DIGITS    		CIFAR     		STL
Target			MNIST-M      		USPS	  		MNIST      		MNIST	  		SVHN      		STL         			CIFAR
Ours (C+VAT)	96.6(0.1)      		97.2(0.2)	   		98.8(0.1)   		97.5(1.5)	   		92.0(0.1) 		80.6(0.2)			69.9(0.8)
Ours (C+L)		96.4(0.1)      		97.0(0.4)	   		98.6(0.1)   		98.2(0.2)	   		93.3(0.3) 		81.4(0.5)			74.1(0.8)

For four out of seven adaptation tasks, our model with L_local significantly outperforms that with VAT loss. For the other three transfer tasks, accuracy with L_local is still comparable to that with VAT loss. 
————————————————————————————————————-

Q2) From Eq.(6), the L_cycle and L_local are the new terms based on the traditional DA. Actually, I have some concern that because of the domain distribution difference, the similarity matrix Wts between target and source data cannot well reflect the true similarity. I understand that the L_dann loss can align the marginal distribution across domains. So, this is an problem of "chicken first or egg first", which depends on the training strategy of the model.

A2) We agree that it can be a problem of “chicken first or egg first” if L_class cannot reduce the distribution discrepancy between the source and the target in feature space. However, we would like to underline that L_class can usually match a significant fraction of them in real transfer tasks. As reported in Table 1 and Table 2, the lowest accuracy that ‘Source Only’ adaptation method achieved is 57.1% and this implies that  L_class alone can align the source and the target features to some extent. Thus, we scheduled L_dann and L_cycle to utilize L_class at the early stage of training and not to make it a problem of “chicken first or egg first”. Moreover, the toy example in Section 4.1 substantiates the effectiveness of L_cycle even when the features are not aligned satisfactorily. We also observed that our model without L_dann achieves comparable performance on various transfer tasks. The experiments were run 5 times.

content.title: General response to all reviewers
content.comment:
We appreciate the reviewers' valuable suggestions and insightful comments. We have revised our manuscript accordingly. We can summarize the major changes made as follows:

1) We cited CAT [1] and added the discussion on it in Section 4.2.
2) We carried out extensive ablation studies on the scale parameter \sigma and the loss function for cycle consistency. These new results are included in Appendix D.
3) We revised Theorem 1 so that it now remains valid under the condition where the source data is slightly perturbed from the ideally clustered condition in Appendix A.1.
4) We clarified our experimental protocol in Appendix B.1.
5) We added a few recent baselines in Table 2 for the Image-CLEF DA dataset experiments. Please note that our method still outperforms most of the baselines compared.

For more details, please refer to our responses to the individual reviewers and the revised manuscript.

Thank you again for your evaluation efforts.

[1] Cluster Alignment with a Teacher for Unsupervised Domain Adaptation. ICCV 2019.

content.title: Official Blind Review #2
content.review_assessment:_checking_correctness_: I assessed the sensibility of the derivations and theory.
content.review:
In this work, the authors propose a new domain adaptation framework through label propagation. Specifically, the labels are propagated using a manifold structure. The clusters of features in each domain are aligned to be close by enforcing the cycle consistency. Moreover, DANN and LGAN is used in the final objective function to align the distribution and enable local manifold consistency. Experimental studies have been done to verify the effectiveness of the proposed method.
Overall, the paper is easy to follow. The idea of label propagation by enforcing the cycle consistency through graphs is interesting. The proof of theorem is simple and correct. My major concern is on the significance of the paper, which is limited. The overall objective consists of four important terms in which L_class, L_dann and L_local are from the existing works. The only contribution is on the L_cycle. However, the cluster alignment idea has been studied in [ref1], while the current work completely ignores [ref1]. Although the ways of aligning the clusters are different between the two works, more discussion and comparison with [ref1] are necessary. Here are some detailed comments:
(1)	The authors claim the scale parameter \delta is learned. Can you show the learned \delta for different domain pairs and discuss how the \delta affects the final performance?
(2)	It is not clear how matrix T and W are associated. It seems that T is the normalized W. However, they are completely in the same form. Why does W still preserve the identity block matrix I after normalization?
(3)	The theorem 1 is for ideally clustered source data, which may not be possible in reality. How the perturbation of unideal clustered source data, e.g., some clusters have overlapping, affect the final performance? The discussion is necessary as this is the case for the complex real-world data.
(4)	Eq.(3) uses L_1 norm. Have you tried any other norms?
(5)	The results of table 1 for the other baselines are directly from the paper. It is not clear whether the same experimental setting is applied, which makes the comparison less convincing. 
(6)	Table 2 demonstrates L may not bring benefits. Although the authors analyse the reason, i.e., the performance of the approximation of the local manifold, it is necessary to give some principled guidelines to guide the usage of L or not when given a new task.
(7)	The comparison with [ref1] should be given. 
(8)	Regarding the selection of the Hyper-parameter in appendix, the authors discuss some possible ways. Which one is used in this work? Is it following (Bousmalis eta al. 2016)? Moreover, why set different ranges for different hyper-parameters? Table 3 shows different tasks use different hyper-parameters. How to set these hyper-parameters given a new task, especially when no target labelled data is available?
(9)	How the batch size is selected? Is it based on the final performance? The transfer performance seems to be sensitive to the batch size. The authors should give more details on this point. 
[ref1] Cluster Alignment with a Teacher for Unsupervised Domain Adaptation.

content.title: Response to Reviewer #2 (Part 3/3)
content.comment:
Q8) Regarding the selection of the Hyper-parameter in appendix, the authors discuss some possible ways. Which one is used in this work? Is it following (Bousmalis eta al. 2016)? Moreover, why set different ranges for different hyper-parameters? Table 3 shows different tasks use different hyper-parameters. How to set these hyper-parameters given a new task, especially when no target labelled data is available?

A8) Regarding the hyperparameter optimization, we followed the protocol of (Bousmalis et al 2016, Saito et al 2017, Rui shu et al 2018) which utilizes a small set of labeled target domain data. In the revised manuscript, we explicitly stated the setting in appendix B.1.
We differentiated the range of hyperparameters, L_cycle and L_local because we concentrated our computational resources on main contribution, L_cycle. We excluded zero from L_cycle coefficient search space whereas included it in L_local coefficient search space for the same reason. We set a greater value for the coefficient of L_local on the target domain than that on the source domain because classification on the target domain is the core objective. Setting different ranges for different hyperparameters can also be found in the literature (Rui shu et al 2018).
In the literature, there seems to be no general methodology on setting hyperparameters when labeled target data is not available at all. However, we found the proposed model is robust to various hyperparameter combinations.

1			96.5			97.4	   		98.6			98.2	  		92.1	       		80.5			69.9

Target			P		I		C		I		P		C
0.01				78.0		90.5		96.4		91.3		76.3		95.3		88.0
0.1				78.1		91.7		96.3		90.6		76.2		96.3		88.2
1				77.8		91.8		95.7		89.7		76.0		95.7		87.8
* L_local was excluded to examine the robustness of the model for changing \beta value. Each experiment was run once because of limited time.
—————————————————————————————————--

Q9) How the batch size is selected? Is it based on the final performance? The transfer performance seems to be sensitive to the batch size. The authors should give more details on this point. 

A9) As described in the appendix, the batch size should be sufficient to prevent any likely bias on the graph. However, we did not tune the batch size for each experiment. We conducted SVHN to MNIST adaptation experiments with various batch sizes up to 384 and observed insignificant performance improvement beyond 128. Consequently, we set the batch size to 128 for all of Digit & Object dataset experiments. For ImageCLEF-DA dataset, our computational resources could not afford the batch size of 128 and we set it to 36 which is the same with the setting of CDAN (Long et al., 2018).

[1] Cluster Alignment with a Teacher for Unsupervised Domain Adaptation. ICCV 2019.

content.title: Response to Reviewer #2 (Part 2/3)
content.comment:
Q3) The theorem 1 is for ideally clustered source data, which may not be possible in reality. How the perturbation of unideal clustered source data, e.g., some clusters have overlapping, affect the final performance? The discussion is necessary as this is the case for the complex real-world data.

A3) We added the extension of theorem 1 which assumes that the source data is slightly perturbed around the ideally clustered condition in Appendix A.1. We achieved the same conclusion with the original theorem 1.
———————————————————————————————————--

Q4) Eq.(3) uses L_1 norm. Have you tried any other norms?

A4) Yes, we tried L_2 norm and cross entropy loss as well. We excluded L_local again to compare the effectiveness of these functions. The experiments were run 5 times. 

		<Accuracy (%) on Digit dataset with different loss functions>
Source		 	MNIST			MNIST	      		USPS	 		SVHN	         	DIGITS     
Target		 	MNIST-M		USPS	       		MNIST			MNIST        		SVHN        
L_1 norm	 	96.5(0.1)      		97.3(0.2)      		98.6(0.1)  		98.2(0.2)       		92.1(0.2)  
L_2 norm	 	96.4(0.2)      		97.1(0.2)      		98.3(0.3)  		98.0(0.1)       		92.0(0.2)  
Cross entropy 	96.3(0.3)      		96.9(0.2)      		98.5(0.2)			96.6(2.9)       		91.8(0.2)  

For all Digit dataset adaptation experiments, evaluating cycle consistency with L_1 norm achieved the highest accuracy. We speculate that L_1 norm is more numerically stable or provides more effective gradients than other functions in this case.
—————————————————————————————————————--

Q5) The results of table 1 for the other baselines are directly from the paper. It is not clear whether the same experimental setting is applied, which makes the comparison less convincing. 

A5) The details about experimental settings are provided in the appendix. We followed the standard protocols for unsupervised domain adaptation (Rui shu et al., 2018, Long et al., 2018). In detail, for Digit dataset adaptation tasks, we used the same architecture with MSTN (Xie et al., 2018). For CIFAR and STL dataset tasks, we used the same architecture with DIRT-T (Shu et al., 2018). In experiments on ImageCLEF-DA, we adopted ResNet-50 architecture. For the adaptation task between MNIST and USPS, we used the training set of each dataset and it is the same with the settings of CDAN (Long et al., 2018). For MNIST to MNIST-M adaptation task, we randomly inverted MNIST images as in SimNet (Pinheiro, 2018). 
—————————————————————————————————————--

Q6) Table 2 demonstrates L may not bring benefits. Although the authors analyse the reason, i.e., the performance of the approximation of the local manifold, it is necessary to give some principled guidelines to guide the usage of L or not when given a new task.

A6) We agree with your suggestion that we need to provide some guidelines for the usage of L_local. We believe that it is manageable to examine the quality of LGAN generator in image domain. It is recommended to use L_local when the generator can adequately approximate local manifolds. 
—————————————————————————————————————-

Q7) The comparison with [ref1] should be given. 

A7)  We cited the reference and added the comparison with it in the revised paper. You can also find the comparison in the below response to Zhijie Deng.

content.title: Response to Reviewer #2 (Part 1/3)
content.comment:
We thank the reviewer for the insightful feedback. We address the detailed comments below.

Q0) The cluster alignment idea has been studied in [ref1], while the current work completely ignores [ref1]. Although the ways of aligning the clusters are different between the two works, more discussion and comparison with [ref1] are necessary.

A0) We agree that the comparison with the suggested work [1] is necessary because both methods focus on learning clustered and aligned features. Though the objectives of the two methods are related, we also would like to point out that the approaches are quite different. Our method utilizes the manifolds of the source and the target domain through label propagation and cycle consistency, whereas CAT considers the distance between two samples for clustering and the distance between the first-order statistics of distributions for alignment. The benefits of utilizing manifold information beyond one to one relations are explained in Section 4.1 of our paper. We cited the paper and added the discussion about it in the revised manuscript.
———————————————————————————————————--

Q1) The authors claim the scale parameter \delta is learned. Can you show the learned \delta for different domain pairs and discuss how the \delta affects the final performance?

A1) Setting an appropriate value for the scale parameter, \sigma, is important because it has a substantial role in determining the transition matrix, T. Therefore, we conducted several experiments with fixing \sigma to various values. For these experiments, we excluded L_local to observe the effect of \sigma. The experiments were run 5 times.

Target				MNIST-M		USPS			MNIST			MNIST			SVHN
\sigma = 0.1			94.8(0.4)			96.5(0.3)			98.3(0.1)			76.7(7.6)			90.6(0.5)	
\sigma = 1			96.4(0.5)			97.2(0.1)			95.8(6.7)			98.2(0.1)			92.0(0.2)	
\sigma = 10 			84.8(3.5)			95.4(0.5)			95.8(0.3)			74.2(4.9)			87.2(0.4)
\sigma = adapt		96.5(0.1)			97.3(0.2)			98.6(0.1)			98.2(0.2)			92.1(0.2)
* The numbers inside parentheses are standard deviations. ‘adapt’ means that the \sigma is learned to adapt according to the embedded features.

For four out of five scenarios, fixing \sigma to 1 performed better than fixing it to 0.1 or 10. The result of adaptively learning \sigma is reported at the bottom row of the table. Compared to fixing \sigma to 1, adaptively learning \sigma achieved better accuracy and had a lower standard deviation range which means that it is more stable. We also would like to highlight that our model is robust to the initial value of \sigma. We conducted extensive experiments with initializing \sigma to 0.1, 1 and 10 and taking it as a trainable variable. The experiments were run 5 times.

Except for SVHN to MNIST transfer task with setting initial \sigma value to 10, the initial value of \sigma has a minute influence to the accuracy. We believe that adaptively learning the scale parameter can be usefully employed in any other graph-based method. The learned \sigma values for various scenarios are as follows.

It seems that \sigma adaptively learns its value according to the transfer task, regardless of its initialization.
———————————————————————————————————--

Q2) It is not clear how matrix T and W are associated. It seems that T is the normalized W. However, they are completely in the same form. Why does W still preserve the identity block matrix I after normalization?

A2) As described in the manuscript, matrix T is the normalized W. More precisely, each row of W is divided by its sum so that the sum of each row becomes 1. Each row of [ Identity matrix; Zero matrix] has only one 1 and the rest of the row are 0s. Accordingly normalizing these rows is the same as dividing them by 1. Thus, W preserves its identity block matrix I after the normalization.

content.title: General response to all reviewers
content.comment:
We appreciate the reviewers' valuable suggestions and insightful comments. We have revised our manuscript accordingly. We can summarize the major changes made as follows:

content.title: Official Blind Review #1
content.review_assessment:_checking_correctness_: I assessed the sensibility of the derivations and theory.
content.review:
This paper proposes an interesting algorithm towards domain adaptation that combines graph learning and label propagation along with cycle consistency. The proposed model is simple and interesting making clever use of labels in the source domain. While the theory is motivated well and seems convincing, I am not entirely sure of the empirical results.
There are no significant improvements of the proposed model over the baselines considered except on STFL-CIFAR data set. An analysis of why this improvement is observed would be good.

I also wonder on how did the cluster quality on the target domain compare with that obtained by the AssocDA baseline. Also coming to the parameter sigma in the Gaussian similarity function, it would be nice to see the values of sigma reported in either the body of the paper or in a supplement.
I will admit I have not thoroughly checked the math in Theorem 1, but the supporting mathematical equations seem plausible.

content.comment:
Q3) Also coming to the parameter sigma in the Gaussian similarity function, it would be nice to see the values of sigma reported in either the body of the paper or in a supplement.

A3) Setting an appropriate value for the scale parameter, \sigma, is important because it has a substantial role in determining the transition matrix, T. Therefore, we conducted several experiments with fixing \sigma to various values. For these experiments, we excluded L_local to observe the effect of \sigma. The experiments were run 5 times.

* The numbers inside parentheses are standard deviations. ‘Adapt’ means that the \sigma is learned to adapt according to the embedded features.

For four out of five scenarios, fixing \sigma to 1 performed better than fixing it to 0.1 or 10. The result of adaptively learning \sigma is reported at the bottom row of the table. Compared to fixing \sigma to 1, adaptively learning \sigma achieved better accuracy and had a lower standard deviation range which means that it is more stable. We also would like to highlight that our model is robust to the initial value of \sigma. content.title: Response to Reviewer #1 (Part 1/2)
content.comment:
We thank the reviewer for the thorough comments and constructive suggestions.

Q1) While the theory is motivated well and seems convincing, I am not entirely sure of the empirical results. There are no significant improvements of the proposed model over the baselines considered except on STFL-CIFAR data set.

A1) As reported in Table 1, our model outperformed the comparison methods on most adaptation scenarios. The improvements over the state-of-the-art are similar in most tasks including USPS to MNIST, DIGITS to SVHN and STL to CIFAR. Moreover, the proposed model achieved a 1.4% margin-of-improvement in C to P transfer task of Image-CLEF DA dataset.
Although the advancements over the baselines may not appear earthshaking, there seems to be no domain adaptation method that shows overwhelming performance in the literature. We thus believe that the outperforming experimental results of our method on various tasks are still significant. In addition, we would like to emphasize that our theoretical finding provides additional support for the effectiveness of our model.
———————————————————————————————————--

Q2) I also wonder on how did the cluster quality on the target domain compare with that obtained by the AssocDA baseline.

A2) The core evaluation metric for domain adaptation is the accuracy on the target task. From this point of view, we believe that how the features with the same label are gathered and the features with different labels are segregated is more meaningful than the cluster quality. As illustrated in Figure 4 and the provided animation, AssocDA (Haeusser et al., 2017) leads some target data to move into the wrong cluster while our model does not. The reason for this is that AssocDA does not consider the relation within the same domain unlike ours. 
In terms of the cluster quality regardless of labels as in unsupervised clustering, AssocDA may be better than ours because it pursues a strict condition that the two-step transition to be uniform within the same class. However, this may drive the features of each class to collapse to one mode and can cause overfitting. As a result, our model significantly outperforms AssocDA as reported in Table 1.
